item.title: How Neo San is processing non-recyclable waste where it is generated
item.description: Bengaluru-based startup Neo San builds compact thermal processing units for dry reject, sanitary and biomedical waste, reducing the need to transport it to distant disposal sites.
item.content:encoded:
Indian cities generate large volumes of non-recyclable dry waste every day, much of which municipal collection systems struggle to manage. Conventional waste management relies on trucks to transport rubbish to distant landfills, dumpsites, and open incinerators. As collection and transport systems struggle to keep pace, large quantities of sanitary, medical and reject waste go untreated, ending up in open burning pits, water bodies or soil as toxic liquid.

Bengaluru-based Neo San is trying to address this problem by processing non-recyclable waste where it is generated, using compact thermal treatment units.

Founded in 2022 by CEO Dhwaj Bagrecha, the cleantech startup grew out of his experience working in urban planning and waste infrastructure. Bagrecha, who holds a degree in Economics and Finance from Jain University in Bengaluru, affiliated with Bangalore University, saw how rising consumption was outpacing municipal waste management systems. This led him to develop equipment that could treat waste on-site.

Processing waste at source

Neo San's product range includes the Neo-X, a wall-mounted unit designed for washrooms and standalone commercial buildings that can process up to 25 kg of waste a day. The Neo-XT handles 150 kg a day and is intended for tech parks, small hospitals, and commercial complexes. Its third model, the AX, is designed for industrial manufacturing plants processing 500 kg or more a day.

The technology uses rapid, high-temperature electric heating based on induction principles. According to the startup, the system reaches 1,200 degrees Celsius within two minutes while consuming minimal electricity.

The thermal process reduces waste to what the company describes as sterile, non-toxic ash. Neo San is also developing hub facilities to collect the residue and convert it into building briquettes.

The startup has two granted patents for its thermal processing technology, with another 13 patent applications pending.

Bagrecha says that on a lifecycle basis, on-site treatment cuts emissions by 98% compared with collection and landfilling. “The savings come from our patented thermal process and from not trucking the waste away,” he says.

Neo San manufactures its hardware in-house and provides software tools for housekeeping staff. It operates as a managed service, maintaining the equipment and sending regular tracking reports to clients' sustainability teams.

Customers can either purchase the machines outright or pay a monthly service fee. The startup serves corporate offices, healthcare facilities, government bodies and commercial real estate clients.

Neo San describes itself as a seed-to-growth-stage startup and has raised Rs 26 crore in total funding. Its clients include Taj, Embassy, and the Government of Karnataka, along with factories and data centres, the startup says.

Over the next year, the company plans to expand its service operations into four additional states and launch a specialised version of the Neo-XT for biomedical waste processing.

Neo San is part of YourStory's Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India's most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru.

item.title: From backup to energy management: how batteries are changing India's power needs
item.description: As electricity demand rises and renewable energy adoption expands, batteries are evolving from backup devices into critical tools for businesses to manage energy use, improve reliability, and build more resilient power systems.
item.content:encoded:
For years, the conversation around batteries in Indian businesses was fairly straightforward: How much backup do you need?


That question is changing.


In conversations with businesses, channel partners, and people working across the energy ecosystem, I have increasingly noticed that the discussion is moving beyond backup duration. Businesses are asking how they can manage their energy better, protect critical operations, integrate renewable power and reduce their dependence on a single source of electricity.


That shift may appear small, but I believe it signals a much bigger change in the role batteries will play in India's energy system. India's electricity demand is entering a structurally higher-growth phase. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), India's electricity demand is expected to grow at an average annual rate of 6.4% between 2026 and 2030, adding more than 570 TWh to annual consumption over this period. Industry is expected to account for around one-third of this additional demand.


At the same time, India's energy mix is changing rapidly. Solar and wind capacity are expanding, businesses are exploring renewable energy, and more industries are looking at ways to control when and how they consume electricity. But renewable generation does not always coincide with consumption. Solar power is abundant during the day, while a business may have significant demand in the evening or at other times.


This is where storage becomes more interesting.


A battery can store energy when it is available and make it available when it is needed. That sounds simple, but at scale it changes how businesses can think about electricity.


For example, a manufacturing unit does not necessarily need a battery only because the grid may fail. It may need storage because a production process cannot tolerate even a short interruption. A commercial facility may need it to manage critical loads. A business using solar may need it to make better use of the energy it generates.


In other words, the battery starts becoming part of the energy architecture rather than simply a backup device. The growth of data centres and artificial intelligence makes this transition even more relevant.


The IEA estimates that global data-centre electricity consumption could almost double from around 485 TWh in 2025 to approximately 950 TWh by 2030. AI-focused data centres are expected to be one of the strongest drivers of this increase.


For these facilities, reliability is not optional. A power interruption can affect computing workloads, cooling systems and critical digital infrastructure. As electricity demand becomes more dynamic, energy storage can provide another layer of flexibility between the grid and the business.


India is already preparing for this shift at the broader system level. The Central Electricity Authority's National Electricity Plan estimates that the country could require around 411.4 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2031-32, including 236.22 GWh from battery energy storage systems. These numbers tell us something important: storage is moving from the margins of the power sector towards its centre.


Earlier, discussions were largely centred on replacing conventional batteries or extending backup time. Now, the conversation is about system design—what loads need to be protected, how much energy needs to be stored, how storage can work alongside existing power infrastructure and whether the system can adapt to future energy requirements.


That is an important distinction.


Not every business needs a large battery system, and storage will not automatically make economic sense for every application. The right solution depends on the load profile, electricity tariffs, grid reliability, renewable generation, operating hours and the cost of the storage system itself.


But businesses are beginning to look at energy as something they can actively manage rather than simply consume.


Technology is making that possible.

(Chirag Chawla is the Founder and CEO of Electrent Energy)

item.title: 7 Books with twisted endings for psychological thriller Fans
item.description: Discover seven psychological thriller books with shocking twists, unreliable narrators and unexpected endings that will keep you guessing.
item.content:encoded:
Psychological thrillers are at their best when they make readers question everything they think they know.

A seemingly trustworthy character may be hiding a disturbing secret, an ordinary relationship may conceal years of manipulation, and a small detail introduced early in the story may completely change the meaning of everything that follows.

For fans of mind games, unreliable narrators and shocking revelations, a predictable ending can be disappointing. The real thrill comes from reaching the final pages and discovering that the story was never quite what it seemed.

If you enjoy books that keep you guessing until the very end, these seven psychological thrillers deserve a place on your reading list. Each offers a gripping mystery, unexpected turns or revelations that can change how you interpret the entire story.

7 Books with twisted endings for psychological thriller fans

1. The Silent Patient by Alex Michaelides

Alicia Berenson is a celebrated painter whose seemingly perfect life changes when her husband is murdered. After the killing, she stops speaking entirely. Years later, psychotherapist Theo Faber becomes determined to uncover what happened and understand her silence.

As Theo investigates Alicia's past, the distinction between truth, memory and obsession becomes increasingly difficult to navigate. The novel's final revelation encourages readers to reconsider the clues scattered throughout the story.

Why read it: Choose this if you love psychological suspense in which the narrator's perspective may be hiding more than it reveals. The ending is especially satisfying for readers who enjoy revisiting earlier chapters with a fresh understanding.

2. Gone Girl by Gillian Flynn

Nick Dunne becomes the prime suspect when his wife, Amy, disappears on their wedding anniversary. The evidence seems troubling, but the couple's marriage is more complicated than it initially appears.

Told through shifting perspectives, the novel gradually exposes the difference between public appearances and private realities. Gillian Flynn explores deception, control and the stories people construct to influence how others perceive them.

Why read it: This is an excellent choice for readers who enjoy morally complicated characters and stories that challenge their assumptions. Its revelations transform the mystery into a disturbing examination of marriage and manipulation.

3. Verity by Colleen Hoover

Lowen Ashleigh, a struggling writer, accepts a job completing a successful author's book series. While working at the author's home, she discovers an unpublished manuscript containing deeply disturbing accounts of the family's past.

As Lowen reads further, she begins questioning what she knows about Verity Crawford and the events surrounding her family. The story builds tension through competing versions of reality, leaving readers uncertain about whom they should believe.

Why read it: Read this if you enjoy disturbing secrets, morally ambiguous characters and endings that leave room for debate. The uncertainty surrounding the manuscript is a major part of the novel's appeal.

10 Psychology books that change how you see daily habits

4. The Housemaid by Freida McFadden

Millie takes a job as a housemaid for a wealthy family, hoping for a fresh start. However, the seemingly comfortable household soon reveals unsettling dynamics, and her new position becomes more complicated than she expected.

As the story unfolds, the characters' motives become harder to read. What initially appears to be a straightforward domestic mystery develops into a tense story about power, secrets and survival.

Why read it: Its fast pace, short chapters and escalating revelations make it a strong pick for readers who want an addictive thriller they can finish over a weekend.

5. Rock Paper Scissors by Alice Feeney

Adam and Amelia travel to a remote location in Scotland in the hope of repairing their troubled marriage. Instead of bringing them closer, the trip creates an atmosphere of suspicion as long-buried secrets begin to surface.

Alternating perspectives and revelations about the couple's relationship gradually complicate the story. The isolated setting adds to the tension, while the narrative encourages readers to question how well spouses can truly know one another.

Why read it: This is a good choice if you enjoy relationship drama mixed with psychological suspense. It rewards readers who pay attention to small details and question what the characters choose to reveal.

6. The Wife Between Us by Greer Hendricks and Sarah Pekkanen

A complicated relationship involving a former wife, a new fiancée and a seemingly charming man sets the stage for this psychological thriller. At first, the situation appears to follow a familiar pattern of jealousy and romantic rivalry.

However, the narrative gradually challenges the assumptions readers make about the characters and their relationships. What appears straightforward becomes a more intricate story of deception, identity and control.

Why read it: Pick this up if you want a thriller that deliberately plays with your expectations. The changing picture of the characters is central to its suspense.

7. Behind Her Eyes by Sarah Pinborough

Louise becomes entangled in the lives of her new boss, David, and his wife, Adele, after a chance encounter leads to an unexpected connection. As she grows closer to both of them, she discovers that their marriage hides troubling secrets.

The story builds through suspicion, complicated loyalties and unanswered questions. Its final developments take the narrative in an unexpected direction, making it particularly suitable for readers who enjoy endings that challenge their understanding of the entire plot.

Why read it: Choose this for a particularly unconventional conclusion. If you enjoy psychological thrillers that push beyond familiar domestic mysteries, this one is worth considering.

Final thoughts

The best psychological thrillers do more than surprise readers with a final revelation. They build believable characters, plant subtle clues and create enough uncertainty to make every discovery feel significant.

Whether you prefer the calculated deception of Gone Girl, the unsettling atmosphere of Verity or the intricate mystery of The Silent Patient, these seven novels offer different approaches to suspense and misdirection.

If you are new to the genre, start with The Silent Patient. If you have already read the popular titles, try Rock Paper Scissors or The Wife Between Us for more relationship-driven mysteries.

item.title: ‘You are all born artists’: Prakash Belawadi on surviving the AI age
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, actor and theatre artist Prakash Belawadi reflected on AI’s impact on creativity and jobs, urging people to reconnect with their inner artist and find purpose beyond what technology can replace.
item.content:encoded:
Actor-theatre artist Prakash Belawadi began his session at TechSparks 2026 with a simple question: “Any artists out there?”

He went on to answer his own question with a profound reflection: “This is a trick question. You are all born artists. But the formal education system and corporate life crushed the artist in you. Reconnect with the artist in you; it will help you survive in this AI age,” he said.

Belawadi spoke on “The last human advantage: What AI cannot replace”, discussing how technology is changing creativity, work, culture, and public life.

Responding to a question about whether AI challenges artists and whether they need to upskill to remain relevant, Belawadi distinguished between art created for personal fulfilment and art produced for commercial or practical purposes.

To illustrate his point, Belawadi asked how many people in the room had tried writing poetry. While few had identified themselves as artists, several hands went up in response to the question about poetry.

“Why would you want to write poetry? You don’t think you’re going to make money out of it. You don’t think it’s going to be a career. Why did you try to write?” he asked.

For Belawadi, the answer lies in the impulse to create something for oneself, without necessarily seeking commercial value or external validation. In such cases, he argued, AI isn't a challenge because the act of creation is the point.

“You write it because you felt like it. You don’t take AI’s help to write poetry,” he added.

However, the equation changes when creativity becomes a professional assignment with a deadline and a specific outcome. For instance, a lyricist tasked with writing a song within four hours could use AI to generate lyrics based on the scene's characters, setting, language, and context.

In these cases, AI becomes a tool for accomplishing a defined objective. As more people turn to it for similar tasks, competition for artists intensifies.

“If you want to do something with art that is useful, I think AI is more than a challenge. We’ll have to look for another occupation, I would say,” Belawadi said.

He acknowledged that actors could also be replaced in certain roles as the technology advances.

“For me as an actor, for instance, at the present level of AI, I can give my persona and charge royalty only for my persona. You can make a non-fungible token of my persona, then just lend it, and AI will do the rest. I don’t need to go to shoot, for instance. I can be replaced,” he said.

Belawadi believes AI cannot easily reproduce a dimension of human experience: the ability to respond to the world through lived experience.

While AI may replicate an actor's appearance and deliver a convincing performance, he believes replacing a person in a conventional screen role could be far easier than replicating the complexity of an individual shaped by lived experience.

“But if you are doing a hero role in a movie, it’s very easy to replace, I think,” he said.

Belawadi pointed out that young people today face a difficult double whammy: climate change and a slew of new technologies.

“There’s a third that’s related to both: you will need two and a half times more energy than you need now when AI is fully deployed, and that is going to make climate change worse. And the new technologies won’t give you jobs.”

Belawadi did not argue for holding back the technology. Asked which human skills beat AI, he turned the question around. “AI can replace many things humans are doing. The question is: what are you doing? Do you need to do that? What are you doing, and why are you doing it?”

He then offered a list of things he thinks AI could take over. It included:

  • Courts: With around 54 million cases pending, he said AI could begin deciding them within seconds. Human judges could retain appeals.
  • Primary health care: Diagnosis and minor procedures at village clinics, with remote guidance for complex surgery, delivered “without prejudice” of caste, gender, skin colour or geography.
  • Elections: If people trust their phones with payments, he asked, why not trust an OTP with a vote?
  • Accounting: He had told his daughter, a chartered accountant, that she was already out of a job.
  • Traffic: He suggested a million driverless vehicles for Bengaluru would give the city back its streets.

Belawadi urged AI developers to use their skills to improve the lives of people around them, arguing that building ethical AI requires a sense of responsibility towards one's community.

“If you are building ethical AI, I think you need to rebel and make a better India. There is no other country that is as good for you as India is, if you have self-respect,” he said.

Emphasising that this responsibility begins with the people in one's immediate surroundings, he added, “When I say India, I don't mean you talk for 1.5 billion people. I'm saying you talk for yourself: whether you can be useful and make lives better for the people around you.”

He cautioned that developers who fail to bring this sense of purpose to their work risk being made redundant by the very technology they create. “Otherwise, I'll talk to AI. I may not need you, I'm saying,” he said.

item.title: Celebrities don't sell, the product does: Ananth Narayanan on what makes a D2C brand last
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, the BRND.ME founder says the growth-hack era is over and the brands that survive will be built on product love, cash flows and global ambition.
item.content:encoded:
The froth has gone out of D2C, and brands that want to last will have to earn it slowly. That was the message from Ananth Narayanan, Founder and CEO of BRND.ME, at the 17th edition of YourStory's TechSparks.

In a fireside chat with Shradha Sharma, Founder and CEO of YourStory and The Bharat Project, Narayanan said the shift towards profitable businesses began two to three years ago. "Without product-market fit, just scaling, which a lot of D2C brands used to do, I don't think is valued anymore," he said. "You need real cash flows, you need real product love, which is very hard."

There is no shortcut, he added, "I don't think there is a get-rich-quick on brand building." In his experience a brand takes seven to 15 years to earn real loyalty and cohorts that last five or ten years. Patient capital is becoming easier to find, he said, through FMCG majors such as Unilever and P&G buying D2C brands, and through a coming wave of IPOs. Founders can help themselves by being frugal. "Most of the large FMCG businesses never took any money. Is it possible for D2C to do the same? I think the answer is yes. It's hard. It's very unsexy."

Think global from day one

Narayanan believes India's next big brands will be built for overseas shoppers. The old barriers of consumer understanding and distribution are easing, he said, with Amazon Global Selling for reach and AI agents trained on Reddit threads and Amazon reviews to stand in for foreign consumers. BRND.ME, which earns more than half its revenue outside India, uses such agents in product development.

His example was Majestic Pure, the group's aromatherapy brand. India is one of the world's top essential-oil producers, and the two biggest aromatherapy brands, doTERRA and Young Living, both American, source over 30% of their production here. Majestic Pure sells comparable products at around $25 against their $65. "It is not the same packaging," he said. "There is a story that you have to learn to tell to command the price premium."

His tip for founders: look at what India exports in bulk, and ask whether a brand can be built on top of it. He named categories like pet care and health and wellness.

Focus, R&D and packaging

BRND.ME has cut down its portfolio to MyFitness, Majestic Pure, Botanic Heart and Party Props. "Our overall business is larger, but the number of brands that we have is smaller," he said. He also called for more real R&D from Indian FMCG firms, citing Botanic Heart's two-year push on efficacy testing so that its claims hold up in the US.

On packaging, he admitted the company still hires a US agency for design. "Packaging is marketing," he said. "You're competing with the Korean brand, the European brand."

"The celebrity may add recall, but the product sells"

On celebrity-led brands, Narayanan was blunt. "A face can give you initial momentum, but I don't think it can get you repeat consumers." Paying an ambassador for a campaign is fine if the return on spend justifies it, he said. Making a celebrity a partner is a different matter, and works only if the star fits the brand and a seasoned business person makes the product, marketing and pricing calls. Otherwise, "you think the celebrity sells, but reality is the product sells." Sharma called it the headline of the session.

Brands that mislead consumers, he said, do not last. "Maybe you can fool consumers once, but I don't think you can fool them again." His advice was to keep 8 to 20% of revenue coming from a brand's own channel, since quick commerce and marketplaces give little feedback, and to be honest about reviews and ratings.

Quick commerce and the cash-flow game

Quick commerce is here to stay, Narayanan said, and works best where speed changes the purchase, as with Party Props. For an FMCG item bought once or twice a month, shelf space is tight and the platforms will take more of the value. He rejected the idea of a monopoly. "There is no monopolistic world in India. If you can compete here, you can compete globally."

He does not judge founders who build to sell, but said that "eventually all valuation games have to be cash flow games, because the only real exit eventually is an IPO." His own aim is a long game. His parting advice to founders was to build with heart: "Build products that you love. Otherwise you are becoming a bit of a machine that churns out unit economics."

Brand India and early-stage funding

Asked how he would pitch India as a brand, Narayanan said it stands for talent today and should now move on to culture, from yoga and Ayurveda to mindfulness. "Why can't we make the Indian way of living the most important thing in the digital age?"

Answering an audience member who said pre-seed D2C funding is hard to come by, he disagreed. "There is a lot of money available if you have a good idea for a consumer brand. In fact, the later stage is much harder. Early stage, it's an idea, and most people like ideas."

item.title: India’s GCCs move up the value chain to build products for global markets
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, leaders from Mercedes-Benz Research and Development India, Siemens Healthineers and Lufthansa Systems India discussed how local problem-solving, product ownership, and innovation can help India build for global markets.
item.content:encoded:
India has long been a global hub for technology services, but its growing engineering capabilities are opening up opportunities to develop products, create intellectual property (IP), and take ownership of innovation. As multinational companies expand their research and development (R&D) centres in the country, Indian teams are moving beyond executing assigned tasks to solving complex problems and building solutions for global markets.

At YourStory’s TechSparks 2026, Manu Saale, Managing Director and CEO, Mercedes-Benz Research and Development India; Kalavathi GV, Executive Director and Head, Global Development Centre, Siemens Healthineers; Luigi Celmi, CEO, Lufthansa Systems India; shared their perspectives on how India’s global capability centres (GCCs) can move up the value chain. The discussion explored the importance of localising products, building domain expertise, and fostering a problem-solving mindset.

For Kalavathi, the shift begins with recognising that healthcare solutions cannot simply be transplanted from one market to another. “What works in the US does not work in India,” she said.

“Our mantra is: Medtech is global, but healthtech is local,” she said, explaining how healthcare solutions must account for differences in lifestyles, disease prevalence, affordability, and access to care.

Previously, companies often adapted products designed for developed markets by removing features to make them suitable for India. But this approach did not adequately address the country's diverse healthcare needs, which span private hospitals, government facilities, and district clinics.

Kalavathi said that affordability and accessibility became essential, along with the needs of both patients and healthcare providers. So, the company began working with Indian clinics, hospitals, and customers to develop solutions tailored to local healthcare needs. “We started co-creating some of the ideas along with the Indian customers,” she said.

One example is a C-arm imaging system that was conceptualised, designed and manufactured in India to address local needs. The product now serves 40 other markets and has an installed base of 1,400 units, she said.

The company has also expanded its engineering capabilities in the country, with around 50% of Siemens Healthineers' software professionals based in India, according to Kalavathi.

For Lufthansa Systems, meanwhile, India's established engineering ecosystem and advances in automation offer an opportunity to build on the capabilities already available within the Lufthansa Group. Although Lufthansa Systems established its India operations only recently, the wider group already has more than 1,000 employees in India across its operations.

“We don't feel that we pay the price to be late. We feel that we can benefit and take the advantage rather of being late,” said Celmi, the company's India CEO, pointing to advances in automation and established industry partnerships.

Bengaluru's expanding aviation and aerospace ecosystem is another draw. In a sector where reliability is critical, engineers must bring deep domain expertise and focus on validating changes. “Engineers spend more time validating changes rather than creating them,” Celmi said.

At Mercedes-Benz Research and Development India, the evolution is from task-based execution to ownership of broader engineering challenges. While the car remains a global product, Manu Saale said, its head unit—the digital interface inside the vehicle—offers opportunities for customisation.

There was a time when India solved tasks based on what was told to them. Now is the time when India is asking, ‘What's the problem? Like, what's the big problem? Give me the big statement, and I try to solve it,’ he said.

Saale said this shift enables Indian teams to take responsibility for entire systems and subsystems rather than depend on daily instructions from global headquarters. As engineers accumulate product knowledge and systems expertise, they can engage with headquarters at a higher level and take ownership of more complex problem statements.

He also emphasised the need for India to move beyond its legacy of technology services and build products for domestic use and export markets. For him, the goal is not simply to connect different layers of technology but to develop the expertise needed to own the entire stack.

This ambition is reflected in the wider GCC ecosystem. Kalavathi cited Nasscom data indicating that 39% of GCCs in India are involved in product development, including product management, while around 9% are transformation hubs.

“We have reached a stage where, given the growth of the ecosystem, we can take ownership of complete products.”

Building original IP also requires companies to start with the problem they want to solve, rather than the technology they want to deploy. Kalavathi said organisations must draw on product expertise, clinicians, customer relationships, and partnerships with hospitals and startups to develop solutions that address unmet needs.

Saale echoed this view, emphasising that innovation begins when teams move from service-oriented thinking to identifying problems and developing solutions.

item.title: Amazon bets on agentic AI to power enterprise ops; Is your marketing AI tool driving profit or just noise?
item.description: Rajeev Rastogi, Vice President of Machine Learning at Amazon, highlighted the rise of agentic AI in the enterprise operating layer. Anand Jain of CleverTap explained why marketing teams must move beyond basic generative AI productivity tools and adopt autonomous, real-time decisioning systems.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

The future points to agentic AI, and its implementation is gathering pace. 

Cognizant and Google Cloud are expanding their partnership to accelerate adoption of agentic AI. This includes a ‘Gemini Frontier Capability Group’, which brings together Google’s full-stack, enterprise-ready AI platform and Cognizant’s industry and engineering expertise as an AI-builder. 

The group will be supported by more than 18,000 dedicated Cognizant associates and a substantial joint investment. 

Meanwhile, ahead of its IPO, Jio Platforms’ anchor book has drawn Rs 2.5 lakh crore in bids. The company allotted 7.24 crore shares at a price of Rs 1,119 apiece to anchor investors, with LIC receiving the largest allocation. 

Moving on, Hunar.AI has raised Rs 40 crore in a Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures. The round also saw participation from Hyderabad Angels Fund, Together Fund, Seedstars, AVNM Ventures, PhysicsWallah co-founders Prateek Maheshwari and Alakh Pandey, and MediaMint co-founder Aditya Vuchi. 

The startup, which develops specialised AI tech for frontline-intensive industries, will use the funds for building AI infrastructure, product development, and go-to-market expansion.

Lastly, a report by Redseer notes that the online retail market in the country is expected to cross $90 billion this year with grocery overtaking mobiles. The gross merchandise value of the ecommerce market expanded roughly 25% year on year to about $38 billion in the first half of 2026, marking its strongest H1 performance in four years.

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • Amazon’s bet on agentic AI to power enterprise ops
  • Marketing AI tool: Is it driving profit or just noise?

Here’s your trivia for today: What was the first Mickey Mouse cartoon ever produced? (Scroll down for the answer)

TechSparks

Amazon bets on agentic AI to power enterprise ops

Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Rajeev Rastogi, Vice President of Machine Learning at Amazon, highlighted the rise of agentic AI in the entire enterprise operating layer, marking a transition from static software to autonomous systems capable of understanding natural language instructions.

“Agents prepare plans dynamically to solve a problem... and invoke the appropriate tools,” Rastogi explained during a fireside chat at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event. 

Driving transformation: 

  • Instead of relying on human intervention at every step, these autonomous agents evaluate queries, formulate a sequence of actions, and call specialised digital tools to complete complex tasks end-to-end.
  • Within Amazon, this operating layer is active in systems like Rufus, a conversational shopping assistant that parses customer requests, applies price filters, invokes search engines, and guides users through product comparisons and checkout journeys. Similarly, autonomous seller assistants pre-fill product listings, monitor inventory levels, and guide small businesses through international export compliance.
  • According to Rastogi, eventually the industry will advance towards genuine world models that possess an internal understanding of physical spaces and environmental behaviour, establishing a practical, cost-effective framework for enterprise automation.

TechSparks

Is your marketing AI tool driving profit or just noise? 

At TechSparks 2026, Anand Jain, Co-founder and Chief Marketing Officer of CleverTap, a customer engagement and marketing automation platform, explained why marketing teams must move beyond basic generative AI productivity tools and adopt autonomous, real-time decisioning systems that drive genuine business profit.

Key takeaways: 

  • In a masterclass on marketing strategy, Jain urged leaders to look beyond simple shortcuts, and move from using AI for fun and games to generating actual business results. 
  • While creating content using AI makes the job faster and saves time, Jain questioned whether it truly drives growth. “Is it actually going to impact business results or is it just more of the same?”
  • Instead of broadcasting generic promotions to large groups, modern marketing engines should interpret live customer actions to match individual needs. This approach marks a shift towards the highest level of AI maturity, known as ‘real-time decisioning’.

  • OYO IPO: OYO parent PRISM plans to nearly halve the size of the fresh issue in its proposed IPO to up to Rs 3,350 crore from almost Rs 6,650 crore. This follows strong cash generation and an improving balance-sheet position, people familiar with the matter told PTI. 
  • Diplomatic visit: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in India on ​Tuesday, days after President Donald Trump delayed tariffs on US imports from India, as ‌the two countries seek to finalise a trade deal. During his two-day visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, Rubio is set to meet government and business leaders.

item.title: Eternal Q2 net profit rises 92% in FY27, revenue up 78%
item.description: Blinkit remained a key contributor to Eternal’s revenue, reporting Rs 19,152 crore in revenue in Q2 FY27.
item.content:encoded:
Eternal, the parent company of Zomato and Blinkit, reported a 92.3% year-on-year (YoY) rise in net profit in the second quarter of FY27, while revenue grew 78% YoY. However, the company missed analysts’ estimates, which had projected a net profit of Rs 250 crore.

Eternal’s net profit for the second quarter of FY27 stood at Rs 125 crore, compared with Rs 65 crore in the same period a year ago. Revenue rose to Rs 24,138 crore from Rs 13,590 crore in the corresponding quarter of the previous fiscal year.

The quick commerce segment, Blinkit, continued to be a key revenue contributor, with revenue reaching Rs 19,152 crore in the second quarter of FY27.

According to Eternal, Blinkit’s net order value (NOV) grew 79.3% year-on-year (YoY). The quick commerce platform added 308 new stores, taking its total store count to 2,751. Its adjusted EBITDA improved for the sixth consecutive quarter, reaching 0.9% of NOV and translating into a profit of Rs 184 crore, compared with a loss of Rs 156 crore in the year-ago period.

Eternal said it expects Blinkit’s store count to exceed 3,500 by March 2027 and potentially reach 5,000 by March 2028.

On the quick commerce business, Eternal Group CEO Albinder Singh Dhindsa said, “How we grow matters as much as how fast. Each of our stores has a finite capacity to serve. A customer who shows up only for a deep discount uses the same capacity as one who orders every week across categories. We could add customers much faster by leaning on price, but those customers usually leave when the discount ends.”

The food delivery business Zomato saw its NOV grow by 21.5% YoY and the company said growth acceleration is now continuing for five consecutive quarters.

On the performance of the food delivery business, Eternal Founder Deepinder Goyal said “We're happy with how the business is doing right now. That said, we try not to read too much into any single quarter. Our long-term expectation for food delivery has always been 20%+ annual growth, and the last two quarters have brought us back to that range. This view didn't change last year when growth slowed, and it doesn't change now that it has picked up.”

Edited by Megha Reddy

item.title: Finance influencer V Harish dies by suicide; father alleges cyberbullying
item.description: The family has accused a venture studio CEO of online harassment. The CEO denies the allegation and says he had questioned Harish's financial regulatory credentials.
item.content:encoded:
(Trigger warning: Story mentions suicide)

V Harish, a financial influencer with over a million followers, has died by suicide at a rented villa near Chennai. His father has alleged that Harish was reportedly “targeted” by Jason Samuel, the CEO of venture studio Zemuria Inc. Harish’s Instagram account was disabled by Meta following allegations made by Samuel, after which he began posting videos on a new handle. Samuel has denied the cyberbullying allegations.

Samuel took to X on Tuesday and wrote, “I am deeply saddened, heavily grieving, shocked and frozen at what has happened and I mourn the loss of life.” 

“I have not cyber-bullied him. I pointed out his lack of license and authority, misrepresentation of license and fraud on SEBI and AMFI where he has not got SEBI RIA for his work and misrepresented that he had an AMFI license when he got the ARN only recently. i.e., his illegal activity.”

He added, “I literally asked him in the video to come back and do this with a proper SEBI license. I never intended or expected this drastic measure to happen and I mourn the loss.”

I am deeply saddened, heavily grieving, shocked and frozen at what has happened and I mourn the loss of life.

I have not cyber-bullied him. I pointed out his lack of license and authority, misrepresentation of license and fraud on SEBI and AMFI where he has not got SEBI RIA for…

— Jason Samuel (@the_jasonsamuel) October 20, 2026

His father claimed that the online dispute had caused stress to the 27-year-old, contributing to his death. He has sought a police investigation into the circumstances surrounding his son’s death, but no case has been registered yet.

According to South First, the Tambaram police have added a charge of abetment to suicide under Section 108 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) in connection with V Harish’s death. Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding his death and the allegations of online harassment made by his family.

item.title: Hunar.AI raises Rs 40 Cr in Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures
item.description: Hunar.AI is focused on developing specialised AI technology for frontline-intensive industries. The company will use the funds for building AI infrastructure, product development, and go-to-market expansion.
item.content:encoded:
Hunar.AI has raised Rs 40 crore in a Series A funding round led by Blume Ventures. The round also saw participation from Hyderabad Angels Fund, Together Fund, Seedstars, AVNM Ventures, PhysicsWallah co-founders Prateek Maheshwari and Alakh Pandey, and MediaMint co-founder Aditya Vuchi.

Hunar.AI will use the funds for building AI infrastructure, product development, and go-to-market expansion. The company is focused on developing specialised AI technology for frontline-intensive industries, where high-volume hiring, geographically distributed teams, and language diversity create operational challenges that conventional HR systems struggle to address.

“Frontline workforce management is one of the largest yet most underserved opportunities in enterprise AI. Solving it requires more than applying general-purpose models to existing processes. It demands a deep understanding of industry workflows, multilingual capabilities and technology that can reliably execute tasks at scale,” said Krishna Khandelwal, Co-founder and CEO, Hunar.AI.

Founded in 2022 by Krishna Khandelwal and Shantanu Bhattacharyya, Hunar’s platform comprises Hunar Voice and Hunar Connect, which use conversational AI agents to manage workforce workflows through voice, WhatsApp and chat. Workflows include candidate sourcing and screening, interview scheduling, onboarding, training, employee engagement and worker retention. By automating high-volume interactions, the platform helps enterprises manage frontline workforce processes while maintaining communication with candidates and employees across locations.

Arpit Agrawal, Partner at Blume Ventures said, “As the world looks to India for lessons in managing these new-age businesses at scale, Hunar is building the AI layer that makes them possible. By focusing on outcomes rather than infrastructure, Hunar has the potential to build a category in India that can scale globally.”

According to a statement, Hunar’s AI agents handled over 15 million conversations in September 2026, with conversation volumes doubling every quarter. Its clients include Swiggy, Delhivery, Instamart, Pronto, Blue Dart, Flipkart, Aditya Birla Capital and Tata Croma.

NITI Aayog projects that India’s gig workforce will grow from around 1 crore workers in 2024–25 to 2.35 crore by 2029–30. As enterprises expand across cities and regions, hiring, onboarding and retaining workers efficiently has become an important operational priority, with many processes still dependent on manual calls, repeated follow-ups and coordination.

item.title: Jio Platforms IPO draws strong demand within hours; Eternal Q2 net profit rises 92%
item.description: The qualified institutional investors showed strong interest for the IPO of Jio Platforms with subscription crossing 4x.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

Jio Platforms’ blockbuster IPO sets the tone for a week in which investor confidence, technology ambitions, and digital trust take centre stage. The Rs 30,213-crore issue drew strong demand from qualified institutional buyers (QIBs) within two hours of opening on Wednesday, with the institutional portion subscribed nearly five times. Jio’s ambitions span telecom, artificial intelligence (AI), cloud and digital services, although retail and non-institutional investor participation remained comparatively muted.

The AI race is also becoming more competitive. OpenAI is expanding beyond its longstanding dependence on Microsoft by bringing its models to Google Cloud, signalling a more diversified approach to computing infrastructure as demand for AI services grows.

But the expansion of AI also raises questions about who sets the rules for the technology. A report highlights the apparent contradiction surrounding OpenAI President Greg Brockman, who advocates AI safeguards even as a political group backed by $25 million from him and his wife opposes regulations that could constrain AI development. The debate underscores the tension between responsible AI development and the industry's push for innovation.

Meanwhile, cybersecurity concerns are putting digital trust under the spotlight. eMudhra is facing scrutiny after weak intermediate certificate authority keys raised concerns about website security. The issue has prompted protective measures from browser operators, while the company has said its Indian digital-signature and eSign services remain unaffected.

Adding to these concerns, a purported leak of 3,897 SBI customer records has raised fresh questions about the security of sensitive financial information and claims of data circulating on the dark web.

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about 

  • Eternal Q2 net profit rises 92% in FY27, revenue up 78% 
  • ‘You are all born artists’: Prakash Belawadi  

Here’s your trivia for today: The RBI once served as the central bank of two other countries. Which were they? (Scroll down for the answer)

News

Eternal Q2 net profit rises 92% in FY27, revenue up 78%

Eternal, the parent company of Zomato and Blinkit, reported a 92.3% year-on-year rise in net profit to Rs 125 crore in Q2 FY27, while revenue grew 78% to Rs 24,138 crore. Blinkit continued to drive growth, with net order value rising 79.3% and adjusted EBITDA turning profitable. However, Eternal's net profit fell short of analysts' estimates, even as its food delivery business recorded 21.5% growth in net order value. 

Key takeaways: 

  • Eternal’s Q2 FY27 net profit rose 92.3% YoY to Rs 125 crore, while revenue increased 78% to Rs 24,138 crore. 
  • Blinkit’s net order value grew 79.3% YoY, and adjusted EBITDA reached Rs 184 crore, compared with a loss of Rs 156 crore a year earlier. The platform added 308 stores, taking its total to 2,751.
  • Net order value at Zomato's food delivery business increased 21.5% YoY, with growth acceleration continuing for five consecutive quarters. 

TechSparks

‘You are all born artists’: Prakash Belawadi on surviving the AI age 

Actor and theatre artist Prakash Belawadi explored what artificial intelligence (AI) can and cannot replace in human creativity and work. He urged people to reconnect with their inner artist and find purpose beyond commercial success. As AI reshapes jobs and industries, he emphasised the importance of lived experience, individual expression and using technology to improve lives.

Key takeaways: 

  • Creativity is not limited to professional artists; creating for personal fulfilment has value beyond money or career prospects, said Belawadi. 
  • While AI can perform many commercially driven creative tasks, human experiences and perspectives remain important distinctions.
  • Developers should use technology responsibly to solve real-world problems, improve lives in their communities and contribute to a better India.

  • AI Monetisation: OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT ads to 26 more countries, taking the total to 89, as it builds its advertising business ahead of a potential IPO. 
  • SpaceX Rally: SpaceX shares rose in premarket trading after revenue growth beat estimates, driven by its AI and satellite businesses. Elon Musk also floated a potential merger with Tesla.

Answer: The RBI served Myanmar until 1947 and Pakistan until 1948.
